duz1: Do flat feet need treatment? Do insoles help children, why does the arch drop later in life, and when should you see a doctor? Six exercises to do at home, and videos.
duz3: Flat feet means that the inner arch of the foot touches the ground when you stand. In most people it causes no problems and needs no treatment; in young children it is normal. If there is pain, if the arch has dropped later in life, or if only one foot is affected, it should be assessed.

duz11: You can check for yourself: stand up and look at the inner side of your foot. If your foot sits completely flat on the ground with no gap, you have flat feet; if the inner edge is raised off the ground, you do not.
duz12: Often there is no obvious cause; it is simply how your feet are, and it can run in families. More rarely it is caused by the bones of the feet not developing fully in the womb, by the tissues being stretched through injury, ageing or excess weight, or by conditions affecting the muscles, nerves and joints.

duz17: If you have none of these, flat feet is just a foot shape.
duz19: Most young children have flat feet. The inner arch of the foot usually develops between the ages of 3 and 10. If your child’s feet are not causing problems, you do not need to do anything.
duz20: On insoles the research is clear: in the Cochrane review of 16 randomised controlled trials (1,058 children), no significant difference in pain was found between custom-made insoles, ready-made insoles and shoes alone in children with painless flat feet. The authors state that they found no evidence supporting costly custom insoles for healthy children without pain. Insoles may help in conditions where the foot is painful, such as juvenile arthritis.
duz21: An arch that drops in adulthood
duz22: The most common cause of flat feet appearing in adulthood is strain and weakening of the tendon that runs behind the inner ankle bone to the sole of the foot and holds the arch up (tibialis posterior). The risk rises with age; it is more common in middle-aged women. Excess weight, diabetes, inflammatory arthritis and a blow or sprain to the area set the scene.
duz23: In this case the first step is to reduce the load: cutting down for a while on the walking and sport that increase the pain, applying ice with a towel in between, wearing a sturdy lace-up shoe and using an insole if needed. If the tendon has torn, surgery may be considered.

duz36: These exercises are for working the muscles that support the arch in painful flat feet. They can be done several times a day; stop any exercise that clearly increases your pain.
duz37: Hold onto a wall or a chair. Take the leg you want to stretch straight behind you and bend your front knee. Keep your back heel on the floor; feel the stretch in your calf.
duz40: Sit with your foot flat on the floor. Tighten the muscles in the sole as if shortening your foot, and raise your arch; do not curl your toes, keep them flat on the floor. Hold for a few seconds and relax.

duz59: Do flat feet need to be treated?
duz60: Usually not. Flat feet generally cause no problems, do not stop you doing sport and are rarely a sign of anything serious. If there is no pain, stiffness, weakness or balance problem, nothing needs to be done.
duz61: My child has flat feet; should I buy insoles?
duz62: Most young children have flat feet; the arch usually develops between the ages of 3 and 10. If there is no problem, nothing needs to be done. The Cochrane review of 16 trials (1,058 children) found no evidence supporting costly custom insoles for healthy children without pain.
duz63: Do insoles correct the arch of the foot?
duz64: No. Insoles, suitable shoes and exercises do not change the shape of the foot; they can, however, ease pain and stiffness. That is why they are recommended only if there are symptoms.
duz65: Can flat feet develop later in life?
duz66: Yes. The tissues of the foot can stretch through injury, ageing or excess weight; in adults the most common cause is weakening of the tendon that runs behind the inner ankle and holds the arch. See a doctor if you did not have flat feet before, or if only one foot is affected.
duz67: When should you see a doctor?
duz68: See a doctor if you have flat feet and any of the following applies to you:
duz69: Your feet are painful, stiff, weak or numb
duz70: You often injure your feet or ankles
duz71: You have problems with walking or balance
duz72: You did not have flat feet before
